The turning of the water into wine at Cana: "⟦Q 138:8.5⟧Tell no man about the water and the wine⟦/Q⟧"
L319.d: During the months when the apostles labored quietly in Galilee, Jesus taught them to preach the forgiveness of sin through faith in God without penance or sacrifice, and that the Father in heaven loves all his children with the same eternal love. At the same time he enjoined them to refrain from discussing three subjects. The work of John the Baptist, the voice at the baptism, and the miracle at Cana were all stories that could stir political excitement or miracle seeking. His instruction to speak only what they had heard from him, not hearsay, shows the principle of witnessing to experience rather than repeating rumors. Jesus sought to divert their minds from miracle seeking to a real and personal experience of the indwelling of God's spirit of love.

L320.t: The Early Organization of the Twelve Apostles
rows: Andrew
Chairman and director general of the twelve
Peter, James, and John
Personal companions of Jesus
Philip
Steward of the group, providing food
Nathaniel
Watched over the needs of the families of the twelve
Matthew
Fiscal agent of the apostolic corps
Thomas
Manager of the itinerary
James and Judas Alpheus
Management of the multitudes
Simon Zelotes
Charge of recreation and play
Judas Iscariot
Treasurer; he carried the bag
L320.d: The twelve early organized themselves by dividing responsibilities among their number. Andrew, the first chosen apostle, became chairman and director general, while Peter, James, and John were appointed personal companions of Jesus, accompanying him even on night vigils of prayer. Philip provided food, Nathaniel cared for the apostles' families, Matthew handled finances, Thomas managed the itinerary, the Alpheus twins managed the multitudes, and Simon Zelotes had charge of recreation and play. Judas Iscariot, the treasurer, carried the bag and made weekly budget estimates for Matthew and reports to Andrew. The practical division suited to each man's temperament and experience is notable, and it is interesting that rest and play were given a place of their own. This organization lasted until the desertion of Judas made reorganization necessary.

L321.t: Four Beatitudes on the Note of Happiness
rows: Happy are the poor in spirit, the humble
Happy are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled
Happy are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth
Happy are the pure in heart, for they shall see God
L321.d: The beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount are based on faith and love, not on law, ethics, and duty, and Jesus started this momentous sermon on the note of happiness. The four beatitudes in this list are attitudes born of faith: poverty of spirit, hunger for righteousness, meekness, and purity of heart. Only the humble hunger for righteousness, and such seekers find the kingdom of heaven within their own hearts now rather than in a distant future. Jesus' righteousness is not the negative thou-shalt-not type but a dynamic love, and genuine meekness has no relation to fear but is the co-operative attitude of "⟦Q 140:5.11⟧Your will be done⟦/Q⟧." Purity of heart refers to the faith man should have in his fellow man. The text also suggests how each beatitude may be taught to children, bringing the teaching down to daily life.

L322.t: Four Supreme Reactions of Fatherly Love
rows: Happy are they who mourn, for they shall be comforted
Happy are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy
Happy are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God
Happy are they who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom
L322.d: Jesus taught that the chief purpose of all human struggling is perfection, even divine attainment, and he admonished his followers to be perfect even as the Father in heaven is perfect. He asked them not to stop at the brotherly love of loving one's neighbor as oneself, but to love men as he had loved them, with fatherly affection. This list gives the four supreme reactions of fatherly love that illustrate this. Mourning is tenderheartedness; mercy is active and dynamic fatherliness; peacemaking is the cure of distrust and suspicion; and enduring persecution is the love that lays down its life for its friends. Fatherly love can freely do things which brotherly love can hardly encompass. A love that delights in returning good for evil is the heart of these beatitudes.

L323.t: Two Great Motives of Jesus' Postbaptismal Mission
rows: To reveal the Father to man
To lead men to become son-conscious, to faith-realize that they are the children of the Most High
L323.d: During the week of rehearsing that followed the ordination, Jesus repeated many times the two great motives of his postbaptismal mission on earth. One was to reveal the Father to man; the other was to lead men to become son-conscious, to faith-realize that they are the children of the Most High. The first is revelation descending from God, the second a realization arising in man. Together they match exactly the two pillars of the gospel of the kingdom: the fatherhood of God and the sonship of man. They may be seen as the man-ward purpose of Michael's bestowal restated for the apostles. Though the apostles failed to comprehend much of his teaching, they did not fail to grasp the significance of the charmingly beautiful life he lived with them.

L324.t: Five Summaries of Jesus' Teaching to Peter, James, and John
rows: Doing the Father's will
Trust in the Father's overcare was not a blind and passive fatalism
Political attitude
"⟦Q 140:8.9⟧Render to Caesar the things which are Caesar's⟦/Q⟧"; avoid political embroilment
Social attitude
Active and spontaneous kindness, expanding the neighborhood to the whole world
Economic attitude
Not an economic reformer, but spiritual values must come first
Personal religion
His teachings are understood by the perfected life he lived
L324.d: Jesus saw that the apostles were still attaching his new spiritual teachings to their old concept of the kingdom as a restoration of David's throne. So one Thursday afternoon he took Peter, James, and John out on the lake in a boat for a four hours' teaching conference, and this list arranges the summary Peter gave Andrew the next morning under five headings. Trust in the Father is not fatalism but active submission; Jesus was neither a political reformer, a sociologist, nor an economic reformer. His concern was the inner spiritual life of the individual, not the mass. Yet while forbidding personal revenge, he approved of the social punishment of evildoers and warned that indiscriminate kindness may cause social evils. Central to the list is the warning never to identify Jesus' teachings with any political or economic system.

L325.t: The Four Burdens of the Passover Message in Jerusalem
rows: The kingdom of heaven is at hand
By faith in the fatherhood of God you may enter the kingdom, becoming the sons of God
Love is the rule of living within the kingdom: supreme devotion to God, loving your neighbor
Obedience to the Father's will, yielding the fruits of the spirit, is the law of the kingdom
L325.d: During the month Jesus and the apostles spent in Jerusalem at the Passover, he or one of the apostles taught daily in the temple. This list gives the four burdens of their message, perhaps the most concise summary of the gospel of the kingdom. It proclaims that the kingdom is at hand, names faith in the fatherhood of God as the condition of entrance, sets love as the rule of living, supreme devotion to God and love of one's neighbor as oneself, and makes obedience to the Father's will, yielding the fruits of the spirit, the law of the kingdom. The structure is clear: entrance by faith, living by love, growth by obedience. Passover pilgrims carried this news to the uttermost parts of the Roman Empire and to the East, and so the gospel began to spread beyond Palestine.

L326.t: Six Phases in the Growth of the God Idea Among the Jews
rows: Yahweh
The god of the Sinai clans, exalted by Moses to the Lord God of Israel
The Most High
El Elyon, proclaimed by Melchizedek to Abraham
El Shaddai
The Egyptian concept of the God of heaven, learned during captivity
Elohim
The Trinity concept of three Gods in one, persisting from the times of Adam
The Supreme Yahweh
By Isaiah's time, a Universal Creator all-powerful and all-merciful
The Father in heaven
A religion wherein the believer is a son of God
L326.d: While in Jerusalem, Jesus mildly upbraided the twelve for not knowing the traditions of Israel relating to the growth of the idea of Yahweh, and then instructed them in the evolution of the concept of Deity throughout the development of the Jewish people. Beginning with Yahweh, the god of the Sinai clans, the idea passed through Melchizedek's Most High, the El Shaddai learned in Egypt, the Trinity concept of Elohim, and the Supreme Yahweh of Isaiah's time, to arrive at last at the Father in heaven. The apostles had never before been so shocked. Jesus pointed out that the Scriptures themselves reveal this growth, as when a later writer attributed to Satan an act that Samuel had ascribed to Yahweh. He also stressed that the Father never fails to accept the sincere worship of his children, however crude their concept of Deity.

rows: You shall worship no other god, for the Lord is a jealous God
You shall not make molten gods
You shall not neglect to keep the feast of unleavened bread
Of all the males of men or cattle, the first-born are mine, says the Lord
Six days you may work, but on the seventh day you shall rest
You shall not fail to observe the feast of the first fruits and of the ingathering
You shall not offer the blood of any sacrifice with leavened bread
The sacrifice of the feast of the Passover shall not be left until morning
The first of the first fruits of the ground you shall bring to the house of the Lord
You shall not seethe a kid in its mother's milk
L327.d: Following his account of the growth of the God idea, Jesus offered this list to show that the understanding of divine law grew in keeping with the enlarging concepts of divinity. When the children of Israel came out of Egypt, before the enlarged revelation of Yahweh, these ten commandments served as their law right up to their encampment before Sinai. Most are ceremonial rules about feasts, first fruits, and sacrifices; the moral demands go little beyond worshiping no other god and resting on the seventh day. Then, amidst the thunders and lightnings of Sinai, Moses gave the new ten commandments, more worthy of the enlarging Yahweh concept. Jesus also noted that the two scriptural records give different reasons for Sabbath keeping, deliverance from Egypt and creation. The lesson is that revelation is not completed at once but grows with human understanding.

L328.t: Seven Facts on Which a True Family Is Founded
rows: The fact of existence
Children take origin in the parents and inherit certain parental traits
Security and pleasure
True fathers take great pleasure in providing for their children
Education and training
Wise fathers prepare their children for the greater responsibilities of later life
Discipline and restraint
Farseeing fathers provide necessary discipline, guidance, and correction
Companionship and loyalty
Always is the father's ear open to their petitions
Love and mercy
Fathers are not like judges, enemies, or creditors; they freely forgive
Provision for the future
Fathers leave an inheritance; death does not necessarily end the family
L328.d: During the Passover season in Jerusalem came Jesus' memorable discussion of the fundamental characteristics of family life and their application to the relationship between God and man. This list gives the seven facts on which a true family is founded. Existence, provision for needs and pleasures, education, discipline, companionship, love and mercy, and provision for the future all mirror the way the heavenly Father deals with his children. The statement that fathers are not like judges, enemies, or creditors but are freely forgiving reaches beyond a legalistic concept of God. Jesus concluded that he had already attained in perfection this entire relationship of a son to the Father, so that in him the way is open still wider for all to see God and become perfect. The family is the nearest analogy for understanding Jesus' concept of God.

L329.t: Three Reasons for the Apostles' Retirement on Gilboa
rows: To confirm their understanding of, and faith in, the gospel of the kingdom
To allow opposition to their work in both Judea and Galilee to quiet down
To await the fate of John the Baptist
L329.d: After a period of work in Galilee and Judea, Jesus and the twelve withdrew for a month of retirement near Mount Gilboa. Jesus made plain that there were three reasons: to confirm their understanding of and faith in the gospel of the kingdom, to allow opposition in Judea and Galilee to quiet down, and to await the fate of John the Baptist. During these September weeks the apostles rested and recounted their experiences, yet they remained divided as to what the kingdom was. Some thought it had already come, others that it was yet to come, and some frankly confessed they were puzzled. Prayer and worship became the central theme of the month, and in answer to Thomas's request Jesus gave his memorable discourse on prayer. The list shows that withdrawal and reflection are as much a part of ministry as activity.

rows: Unselfish
Not alone for oneself
Believing
According to faith
Sincere
Honest of heart
Intelligent
According to light
Trustful
In submission to the Father's all-wise will
L330.d: When the apostles asked for a model prayer, Jesus gave them the one he had prayed with his family in Nazareth and then named five qualities of effective prayer. Each item is a single word with a short gloss: unselfish, believing, sincere, intelligent according to one's light, and trustful in submission to the Father's all-wise will. The first four shape the attitude of the one who prays; the fifth places every petition under the Father's will. Jesus never taught a formal personal prayer, and on the mountain he prayed mainly for his disciples while engaging much in worshipful communion with his Father. The list shows that the attitude of the one praying, not the wording, determines whether prayer is effective.

L331.t: Sixteen Points on Prayer and Worship at Jotapata
rows: Persistent regard for iniquity gradually destroys the prayer connection
Prayer inconsistent with God's laws is an abomination
Opening the human end makes divine ministry available; synchrony of forgiveness
A basic law of justice which mercy is powerless to circumvent
They who would receive mercy must show mercy
Wholly dedicated to the Father's will, all petitions are answered
Prayer changes man's attitude; the motive gives it right of way
Prayer may not be employed to avoid delays of time or handicaps of space
Ask in my name; guard against self-centered prayers
Petitions do not take the place of loving and intelligent ministry
Not only when in trouble; "⟦Q 146:2.12⟧Nevertheless, your will be done⟦/Q⟧"
Pray for the extension of the kingdom; prayer and offending speech
Prayer for divine guidance, a prayer for divine wisdom
Not ornate repetitions or fasting, but thanksgiving leading to true worship
Be not overanxious; spread your needs before the Father with thanksgiving
Remain in silent receptivity so the indwelling spirit may speak
L331.d: At Jotapata Nathaniel was confused about the Master's teachings on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship, and Jesus answered the twenty-four at great length. The revelators summarize the discourse in modern phraseology as sixteen points. The early points describe what blocks prayer: harboring iniquity, petitions inconsistent with God's laws, and a law of justice that mercy cannot circumvent. The middle points give prayer its right direction: dedication to the Father's will, the motive behind a petition, and guarding against self-centered asking. The last points move through thanksgiving to worship, ending with silent receptivity so the indwelling spirit may speak. Two insights stand at the center: prayer does not change God's attitude toward man but man's attitude toward God, and worship makes one increasingly like the being who is worshiped.

L332.t: Six Levels of Interpreting the Rule of Living
rows: The level of the flesh
A purely selfish and lustful interpretation
The level of the feelings
Sympathy and pity enhance the interpretation
The level of mind
The highest idealism embodied in profound self-respect
The level of brotherly love
Unselfish devotion to the welfare of one's fellows
The moral level
As a wise and impartial third person would interpret it
The spiritual level
The divine command to treat all men as God would treat them
L332.d: When Nathaniel asked whether the golden rule might be misjudged by men of evil intent, Jesus taught that one rule of living carries differing levels of meaning according to the one who interprets it. At the level of the flesh it can excuse selfish lust; through the levels of feelings and mind it rises to brotherly love and unselfish social service; on the moral level one views it as a wise, impartial third person would. At the spiritual level it becomes the divine command to treat all men as we conceive God would treat them, the universe ideal of human relationships. The six levels form an ascending ladder. Nothing Jesus had said up to that time more astonished the apostles, who learned that his commonplace teachings require a genuinely spiritual interpretation.

L333.t: Ten Teachings on Magic and Superstition
rows: Astrology
The courses of the stars have nothing to do with human events
Internal organs of animals
Reveal nothing about weather, future events, or human affairs
Spirits of the dead
Do not come back to communicate with the living
Charms and relics
Impotent to heal disease, ward off disaster, or influence evil spirits
Casting lots
Not a method designed to disclose the divine will
Divination, sorcery, witchcraft
Superstitions of ignorant minds; magic numbers and omens unfounded
Interpretation of dreams
Largely a superstitious and groundless system of speculation
Idols
Nothing more than the material of which they are made
Enchanters, wizards, magicians, sorcerers
Derived from ancient superstitions; amulets and incantations futile
Spells, cursing, mandrakes, knotted cords
Exposed and denounced as enslaving superstition
L333.d: When Andrew asked whether a bright new star truly signaled the birth of a great man, Jesus entered upon a thoroughgoing discussion of human superstition, summarized here in ten statements. He addresses astrology, reading the organs of slain animals, communication with the spirits of the dead, charms and relics, casting lots, divination and sorcery, the interpretation of dreams, idols, the practices of ancient enchanters, and spells and curses. He affirms astronomy as a proper pursuit of science while calling astrology a mass of superstitious error. The heart of the list is that the only means of communion with the spiritual world is the spirit endowment of mankind: the indwelling spirit of the Father, the outpoured spirit of the Son, and the influence of the Infinite Spirit. The gospel frees men from enslaving superstition.

L334.t: Four Views of Jesus Held at Capernaum
rows: A deluded and harmless religious fanatic
A dangerous and designing agitator who might stir up rebellion
In league with devils, perhaps even a prince of devils
Beside himself, mad, mentally unbalanced
L334.d: As Jesus' teaching stirred Galilee, fifty leading citizens of Capernaum met at the synagogue to discuss the momentous question, "⟦Q 154:4.1⟧What shall we do with Jesus⟦/Q⟧?" They debated past midnight without agreement. Apart from a few who thought he might be the Messiah or a prophet, the meeting split into four nearly equal groups. They saw him as a harmless fanatic, a dangerous agitator, an ally of devils, or a man mentally unbalanced; each view misses who he truly was. The revelators add that his enemies called his teachings impractical, a charge repeated by later generations, yet the world has never seriously tried to carry out the teachings of Jesus on a large scale, and a much better civilization could be built upon them. The list shows typical human reactions to unfamiliar truth.

L335.t: Three Distinct Forms of Religious Devotion
rows: Primitive religion
The instinctive urge to fear mysterious energies; the religion of fear
The religion of civilization
The religion of the mind; intellectual theology of established tradition
True religion—the religion of revelation
The religion of the spirit as demonstrated in human experience
L335.d: On the way to Phoenicia Jesus taught that the religions of the world have a double origin, natural and revelatory, and that among any one people three distinct forms of religious devotion are found together. Primitive religion springs from fear of mysterious energies; the religion of civilization is the religion of the mind, an intellectual theology resting on the authority of tradition; true religion is the religion of revelation, the religion of the spirit demonstrated in human experience. Jesus refused to belittle primitive worship, but he contrasted the easy refuge of authority, which asks only intellectual assent, with the religion of the spirit, which means effort, struggle, faith, and progress. He then challenged the twenty-four to choose between fossilized conformity and the adventure of proclaiming the new truths of the spirit.

L336.t: Two Demonstrations That You Are God-Knowing
rows: The fruits of the spirit of God showing forth in your daily routine life
Your entire life plan risked unreservedly on the adventure of survival after death
L336.d: Jesus warned the apostles not to try to prove to other men that they had found God, for such proof cannot be consciously produced. Instead he named two positive and powerful demonstrations that one is God-knowing. The first is the fruits of the spirit of God showing forth in daily routine life. The second is a whole life plan that has unreservedly risked everything on the adventure of survival after death in the hope of finding the God of eternity. One is evidence in daily character, the other in the direction of an entire life. The Father responds to the faintest flicker of faith, but those called out of darkness into light are to believe with a whole heart. Their religion is not a theologic shelter but real experience that testifies God has found them.

L337.t: Three Ways of Contending with and Resisting Evil
rows: To return evil for evil
The positive but unrighteous method
To suffer evil without complaint and without resistance
The purely negative method
To return good for evil, to overcome evil with good
The positive and righteous method
L337.d: When Jesus told the apostles to offer the other garment to one who unjustly took their coat, he meant not a literal second coat but doing something positive to save the wrongdoer, in place of the old advice to retaliate, "⟦Q 159:5.11⟧an eye for an eye⟦/Q⟧." He abhorred both retaliation and becoming a merely passive victim of injustice. So he set three ways of contending with evil side by side. Returning evil for evil is positive but unrighteous; suffering evil without complaint is purely negative; returning good for evil and asserting the will to become master of the situation is the positive and righteous method. The story of carrying the pack a second mile illustrates this third way. The list distinguishes Jesus' active righteousness from mere nonresistance.

L338.t: Four Essential Factors of the Higher Levels of the Art of Living
rows: Mutual self-expression and self-understanding
Recognition and appreciation are essential to the development of character
Union of souls—the mobilization of wisdom
One mind augments its spiritual values by gaining the insight of another
The enthusiasm for living
Isolation exhausts the soul; friendship enhances the joys of life
The enhanced defense against all evil
Personality association and mutual affection are an efficient insurance against evil
L338.d: Rodan, the Greek philosopher of Alexandria, lectured Nathaniel and Thomas on the art of living and explained why associations of friendship and mutual affection are socializing and ennobling. He named four factors: mutual self-expression and self-understanding, the union of souls that mobilizes wisdom, the renewal of enthusiasm for living that isolation exhausts, and an enhanced defense against evil, which is more painful when borne alone. He pointed out that the Master never sends his followers out alone but always two and two. Rodan held that such association finds its ideal possibilities in the marriage relation, and that small, trustworthy units of human association, assembled in the aggregate, could produce the civilization of mortal maturity. The point of the list is that association, not isolation, develops personality.

L339.t: Six Essentials of the Temporal Life according to Rodan
rows: Good physical health
Clear and clean thinking
Ability and skill
Wealth—the goods of life
Ability to withstand defeat
Culture—education and wisdom
L339.d: Rodan's second lecture turns from spiritual ideals to the practical conditions of temporal life. He names good physical health, clear and clean thinking, ability and skill, wealth, the ability to withstand defeat, and culture, meaning education and wisdom. The list moves from the body through the mind and practical skill, then to material goods, emotional resilience, and culture. Rodan held that even problems of bodily health are best solved from the standpoint of the Master's teaching that body and mind are the dwelling place of the spirit of God. He also observes soberly that faithfulness in daily work does not insure wealth, for material rewards flow in certain well-organized channels, so wise planning is essential to worldly prosperity. The list balances the spiritual and the practical life.

L340.t: Nathaniel's Five Steps of Reasoning on the Personality of the Father
rows: The Father enjoys equality of communication with the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit
Jesus, equal with the Father, manifested personality; so all three Godheads possess personality
The personality of Jesus demonstrated the personality of God and God's presence in man
Personality and God are both man's highest concept; so God is an infinite personality
God must be a personality since he is the Creator and destiny of all personality
L340.d: Thomas and Nathaniel debated with Rodan, a Greek philosopher who found it hard to think of God as a person. By Monday night Thomas gave up, but by Tuesday night Nathaniel had won Rodan through five steps of reasoning. He began with the Father's equality of communication with the other persons of the Trinity, then argued from the personality that Jesus manifested to his earth children and from Jesus' understanding communication with both God and man. He closed with a philosophical argument that personality is man's highest concept, and the conclusion that God is the Creator and destiny of all personality. Rodan confessed that while God must be infinitely more than a personality, he cannot be anything less, and he accepted Jesus as the personal revelation of the Father.

L341.t: Nine Points on the Divine Nature of Jesus
rows: Jesus has admitted his divinity, and we believe him
His life association with us exemplifies the ideal of human friendship
He never does wrong; he is consistently sinless
The uniqueness of his character and the perfection of his emotional control
He knows men's thoughts and has a superhuman consciousness of Deity
The phenomenon of his superhuman knowledge
He asserts his superhumanity and speaks with the authority of a divine teacher
He talks about God as an ever-present associate; he and the Father are one
In his prayer life he appears to communicate directly with his Father
L341.d: One point remained: the divine nature of Jesus, a doctrine only recently announced in public. Nathaniel and Thomas jointly presented their views, and the revelators give a condensed, rearranged, and restated version in nine points. The grounds come from the apostles' experience of living with him. He is a blameless friend, never repents because he transgresses no law, has perfect emotional control, knows men's thoughts, shows superhuman knowledge, speaks with divine authority, says with childlike naturalness that he and the Father are one, and prays as if face to face with God. The apostles conclude that he is either the greatest fraud the world has known or just what he claims to be. The list ends with their conviction that he is the Son of Man and the Son of God.

L342.t: Seven Points in Jesus' Last Talk with the Seventy
rows: The gospel must be proclaimed to all the world, to gentile as well as to Jew
While ministering to the sick, refrain from teaching the expectation of miracles
Proclaim a spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God, not an outward kingdom
Avoid loss of time through overmuch social visiting and other trivialities
If the first house proves a worthy home, abide there throughout the sojourn
The time for an open break with the religious leaders at Jerusalem has come
Man's whole duty is summed up in loving God and your neighbor as yourself
L342.d: On the morning the seventy went forth on their first mission, Jesus spoke with them for the last time at the Magadan Camp and emphasized seven points. The gospel is for all the world; the sick are to be ministered to without teaching the expectation of miracles; and the message is a spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God, not an outward kingdom of worldly power. Practical counsel follows about avoiding wasted time and abiding in one worthy home, along with the announcement that the time for an open break with the religious leaders at Jerusalem had come. The last point replaces the 613 rules of living expounded by the Pharisees with one commandment of love for God and neighbor. The list gathers the scope, content, and spirit of the mission.

L343.t: Six Virtues Peter Exhorted the Seventy to Cherish
rows: Consecrated devotion
Pray always for more laborers; neglect not daily worship
True courage
They would meet hostility and persecution; no undertaking for cowards
Faith and trust
Go forth unprovided for; trust the Father for all things needful
Zeal and initiative
Intelligent enthusiasm; attend strictly to their Master's business
Kindness and courtesy
Courtesy toward all; do not leave a modest home
Ministry to the sick
Search out the sick in mind and body
L343.d: After Jesus' last talk with the seventy, Simon Peter took them aside and preached their ordination sermon, an elaboration of the charge the Master gave when he laid his hands upon them and set them apart as messengers of the kingdom. The sermon is built on six virtues. Devotion, courage, and faith and trust shape the inner attitude of the messenger, while zeal and initiative, kindness and courtesy, and ministry to the sick govern how he treats people. The instruction to "⟦Q 163:4.13⟧salute no man by the way⟦/Q⟧" was not a call to rudeness but a common idiom against wasting time on lengthy Oriental salutation. Peter warned of persecution, yet none withdrew, and they went out two and two into Galilee, Samaria, and Judea. The list translates the Master's charge into practical terms.

L344.t: Three Questions for All Who Acquire Great Wealth
rows: How much wealth did you accumulate?
How did you get this wealth?
How did you use your wealth?
L344.d: While teaching about wealth, Jesus was asked by a bystander how the wealthy would stand in the day of judgment. He replied that he had come to judge neither the rich nor the poor, but that the lives men live will sit in judgment on all. He then named three questions that must at least be answered by all who acquire great wealth. How much was accumulated concerns quantity; how it was gotten concerns the rightness of the means; how it was used concerns stewardship. The heart of the list is its balance: wealth itself is not condemned, yet accumulation, acquisition, and use are all held to account. The three questions offer a concise standard for self-examination. Having said this, Jesus went into his tent to rest before the evening meal.

L345.t: Three Things to Which the Pharisees Paid Particular Attention
rows: The practice of strict tithing
Scrupulous observance of the laws of purification
Avoidance of association with all non-Pharisees
L345.d: At a Sabbath breakfast given by Nathaniel, a wealthy Pharisee of Ragaba, the host was shocked that Jesus did not wash his hands before eating. In explaining the scene, the revelators note that there were just three things to which the Pharisees paid particular attention: strict tithing, scrupulous observance of the laws of purification, and avoidance of association with all non-Pharisees. All three focus on outward acts and a separated status. On this occasion Jesus sought to expose the spiritual barrenness of the first two practices, rebuking those meticulous in tithing who shun justice, spurn mercy, and reject truth. His rebuke of their refusal to associate with non-Pharisees he reserved for a later occasion when he would again dine with many of the same men.

L346.t: Three Groups of Events Which May Occur in Your Lives
rows: Normal happenings which are a part of the life you and your fellows live
Accidents of nature or mischances of men, in no way prearranged by spiritual forces
The harvest of your direct efforts to comply with the natural laws
L346.d: On the way to Philadelphia Thomas asked whether spirit beings produce strange events or prevent accidents. Jesus called it superstition to see prosperity as divine approval and adversity as God's displeasure; the eighteen killed by the tower of Siloam were no worse offenders than others. He then sorted the events of life into three groups: normal happenings shared by all, accidents of nature or mischances of men that are in no way prearranged by spiritual forces, and the harvest of efforts to comply with natural laws. He illustrated the third with a fig tree parable and declared that health is not the smile of heaven, neither is affliction the frown of God. The Father bestows material blessings without discrimination, but spiritual gifts are limited by man's faith.

rows: A genuine and sorrowful sympathy for Martha and Mary
Perturbed by the crowd of mourners, some sincere and some merely pretenders
He hesitated about summoning Lazarus back to experience bitter persecution
L347.d: On the way to the tomb of Lazarus at Bethany, Jesus wept. The revelators candidly admit that, although they have access to the record of combined human emotions and divine thoughts in the mind of the Personalized Adjuster, they are not altogether certain of the real cause. They name three thoughts and feelings that were going through his mind: deep human affection for the grieving sisters, distress at a crowd of mourners mixing the sincere with mere pretenders, and hesitation about bringing his friend back to mortal life only to face persecution. The scene shows that one wielding divine power also possessed genuine human emotion. The narrative then turns to the stage being set for the greatest manifestation of divine power during his incarnation in the flesh.

rows: Prayer is an expression of the finite mind in an effort to approach the Infinite
When a prayer is apparently unanswered, the delay often betokens a better answer
Prayers indited by the spirit may be answered only in eternity
Answers may be recognized only after the praying mind attains the immortal state
Prayers distorted by ignorance are translated by intervening spirit beings
True prayers are addressed to spiritual beings and answered in spiritual terms
No prayer can hope for an answer unless born of the spirit and nurtured by faith
The child may petition; the parent may delay, modify, or postpone the answer
Answers will be on deposit, awaiting future spiritual levels of attainment
All genuine spirit-born petitions are certain of an answer
L348.d: On the way from Bethany to Pella the apostles asked many questions about prayer, troubled that Jesus had said Lazarus's sickness was not to the death when he had already died. The revelators summarize Jesus' answers in ten points. Prayer is the effort of the finite mind to approach the Infinite, so its answer is conditioned by the vision of the Infinite and by the time-space factor. Delayed or unseen answers may be better answers, answers possible only in eternity or recognizable only in the immortal state, or prayers translated by spirit beings. Yet no sincere prayer is denied an answer; answers wait on deposit until we reach the spiritual level where we can recognize them. The figure of child and parent ties the teaching together with warmth.

L349.t: Four Objections to the Master's Teachings
rows: He is a friend of publicans and sinners; he eats with the ungodly
He is a blasphemer; he talks about God as being his Father
He is a lawbreaker; he heals disease on the Sabbath
He is in league with devils; he works wonders by the power of Beelzebub
L349.d: After the raising of Lazarus, hostility toward Jesus began to harden into formal charges. The Pharisees and chief priests crystallized their objections to his teachings on four grounds: he is a friend of publicans and sinners and eats with them; he is a blasphemer who calls God his Father and thinks himself equal with God; he is a lawbreaker who heals on the Sabbath; and he is in league with devils, working wonders by the power of Beelzebub. The first charge is social, the second theological, the third legal, and the fourth spiritual. Ironically, the first three point to what Jesus actually did and taught, yet his accusers read these things as sin. The list foreshadows the accusations that would later be brought at his trial.

L350.t: Four Concepts of the Kingdom Before Jesus
rows: A present reality
As the prophets presented the kingdom of God
A future hope
Realized in fullness upon the appearance of the Messiah; taught by John the Baptist
The later Jewish concept
A world-wide and transcendental kingdom of supernatural origin and miraculous inauguration
The Persian teachings
A divine kingdom as the triumph of good over evil at the end of the world
L350.d: In recounting Jesus' Sabbath afternoon sermon on the kingdom at Pella, the revelators first set out the background ideas. The Hebrew prophets presented the kingdom of God with a dual concept, as a present reality and as a future hope to be realized with the Messiah. Two further ideas must be borne in mind: the later Jewish concept of a world-wide kingdom of supernatural origin and miraculous inauguration, and the Persian teaching of the triumph of good over evil at the end of the world. Just before Jesus came, the Jews combined and confused all of these into an apocalyptic hope of Jewish triumph. In choosing this concept, Jesus appropriated the most vital heritage of both religions and filled an old vessel with new meaning.

L351.t: Four Distinct Groups of Ideas of the Kingdom of Heaven
rows: The concept of the Jews
The concept of the Persians
The personal-experience concept of Jesus—"⟦Q 170:1.11⟧the kingdom of heaven within you⟦/Q⟧"
The composite and confused concepts of the founders and promulgators of Christianity
L351.d: Down through the centuries of the Christian era the kingdom of heaven has been both understood and misunderstood, and the revelators sort the ideas mixed into it into four distinct groups. There is the Jewish concept of messianic triumph, the Persian concept of good overcoming evil at the end of the world, the personal-experience concept of Jesus himself, and the composite and confused concepts impressed upon the world by the founders and promulgators of Christianity. Only the third belongs to Jesus, while the fourth results from entangling the others. In his public teaching Jesus may have presented numerous concepts of the kingdom, but to his apostles he always taught it as man's personal experience in relation to his fellows and to the Father in heaven. His last word was always, "⟦Q 170:1.13⟧The kingdom is within you⟦/Q⟧."

L352.t: Three Factors in the Confusion about the Kingdom of Heaven
rows: Observing the idea as it passed through the progressive phases of its recasting by Jesus and his apostles
The transplantation of early Christianity from a Jewish to a gentile soil
Christianity organized about Jesus' person; the gospel became a religion about him
L352.d: For centuries the meaning of the term kingdom of heaven has been surrounded by confusion, and the revelators trace it to three factors. The first is the confusion that came from watching the idea pass through the progressive phases of its recasting by Jesus and his apostles. The second is the confusion inevitably associated with transplanting early Christianity from a Jewish to a gentile soil. The third is the confusion inherent in the fact that Christianity became a religion organized about the central idea of Jesus' person, so that the gospel of the kingdom became more and more a religion about him. That last factor echoes the book's recurring distinction between the religion of Jesus and a religion about Jesus.

L353.t: Seven Endowments of the New Life of Spiritual Liberty
rows: New courage and augmented spiritual power; to dare to hope for eternal life
A message of new confidence and true consolation for all men, even the poor
A new standard of moral values, a new ethical yardstick for human conduct
The pre-eminence of the spiritual compared with the material
Spiritual attainment held up as the true goal of living
Eternal realities as the result (reward) of righteous earthly striving
Salvation as the revelation of a divine purpose in the endless service of the salvaged sons
L353.d: In his sermon at Pella, Jesus made it clear that the kingdom of heaven must begin with, and be centered in, the dual concept of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Accepting this teaching would liberate man from the age-long bondage of animal fear and enrich human living with seven endowments of the new life of spiritual liberty. They are courage and spiritual power, consolation even for the poor, a new moral and ethical yardstick, the pre-eminence of the spiritual over the material, spiritual attainment as the true goal of living, eternal realities as the reward of righteous striving, and a destiny of endless service. This expanded idea of the kingdom was hardly embraced in the elementary teachings of John the Baptist.

L354.t: The Apostles' Double Viewpoint of the Kingdom
rows: A matter of personal experience then present in the hearts of true believers
A question of racial or world phenomena; in the future, something to look forward to
L354.d: By the time of the sermon at Pella the apostles had acquired a double viewpoint of the kingdom. They regarded it as a matter of personal experience already present in the hearts of true believers, and as a question of racial or world phenomena, something in the future to look forward to. They expected the kingdom in men's hearts to grow gradually, like leaven, but its world coming to be sudden and spectacular. Jesus never tired of telling them that the kingdom was their personal experience of realizing the higher qualities of spiritual living. That afternoon he taught a new double concept: the kingdom of God in this world, the desire to do God's will, and the kingdom of God in heaven, where love for God is perfected.

L355.t: Two Things Essential to Faith-Entrance into the Kingdom
rows: Faith, sincerity
To come as a little child, receive sonship as a gift, be open-minded and teachable
Truth hunger
The thirst for righteousness, a change of mind, the motive to be like God and to find God
L355.d: Jesus taught that by faith the believer enters the kingdom now, and in various discourses he named two things essential to faith-entrance. The first is faith and sincerity: to come as a little child, to receive the bestowal of sonship as a gift, to submit to the Father's will in full confidence in his wisdom, and to be open-minded and teachable. The second is truth hunger: the thirst for righteousness, a change of mind, and the motive to be like God and to find God. Jesus went on to teach that sin is the offspring of a knowing mind dominated by an unsubmissive will, and that forgiving our fellows creates the capacity to receive God's forgiveness. The door of the kingdom opens to childlike trust and hunger for truth.

L356.t: The Kingdom Steps of Inner Righteousness
rows: God's forgiveness is experienced just in so far as man forgives his fellows
Man will not truly forgive his fellows unless he loves them as himself
To thus love your neighbor as yourself is the highest ethics
Moral conduct, true righteousness, becomes the natural result of such love
L356.d: The revelators explain that the righteousness of the kingdom is revealed in the technique of receiving God's forgiveness. Faith is the price of entrance into the family of God, and forgiveness is the act of God which accepts that faith as the price of admission. The actual experience of forgiveness unfolds in four steps. God's forgiveness is experienced as one forgives one's fellows; true forgiveness requires loving them as oneself; such love is the highest ethics; and true righteousness is the natural result of that love. Jesus did not put ethics in the place of religion; he taught religion as a cause and ethics as a result. Righteousness, the list implies, is not the effort of rule-keeping but the fruit that flows naturally from love.

L357.t: Five Phases, or Epochs, of the Kingdom
rows: The inward experience of the individual believer's fellowship with God the Father
The enlarging brotherhood of gospel believers; enhanced morals and quickened ethics
The supermortal brotherhood of invisible spiritual beings on earth and in heaven
The more perfect fulfillment of the will of God—the next age of man
The kingdom in its fullness, the future spiritual age of light and life
L357.d: Jesus never gave a precise definition of the kingdom; at different times he discussed different aspects of it. In his Sabbath afternoon sermon at Pella he noted no less than five phases, or epochs. They begin with the inward experience of the individual believer, then extend to the social brotherhood of believers, the superhuman kingdom of invisible spiritual beings, the next age of man in which the will of God is more perfectly done, and finally the kingdom in its fullness, the age of light and life. The revelators advise that we must always examine which of these five phases the Master means when he uses the term kingdom of heaven. The list is a practical key for reading the Gospels.

L358.t: Five Cardinal Features of the Gospel of the Kingdom
rows: The pre-eminence of the individual
The will as the determining factor in man's experience
Spiritual fellowship with God the Father
The supreme satisfactions of the loving service of man
The transcendency of the spiritual over the material in human personality
L358.d: In the same sermon at Pella, Jesus emphasized five points as the cardinal features of the gospel of the kingdom: the pre-eminence of the individual, the will as the determining factor in experience, spiritual fellowship with God the Father, the supreme satisfactions of loving service, and the transcendency of the spiritual over the material in personality. Fellowship with God reaches upward and service to man reaches outward. The revelators note that the world has never seriously tried out these dynamic ideas, yet they urge us not to be discouraged by slow progress, since evolution is subject to sudden changes. Nor should we, while awaiting the age manifestation of the kingdom, fail to establish it within our own souls.

L359.t: Two Great Tendencies That Modified the Master's Concept of the Kingdom
rows: Jewish believers regarded him as the Messiah who would soon return to establish a material kingdom
Gentile Christians accepted Paul's doctrines; Jesus as Redeemer of the children of the church
L359.d: The ideas and ideals of Jesus in the gospel of the kingdom nearly failed of realization as his followers progressively distorted his pronouncements. The revelators sum up that distortion in two great tendencies. The Jewish believers persisted in regarding him as the Messiah who would very soon return to establish a world-wide and more or less material kingdom. The gentile Christians early accepted the doctrines of Paul and came to believe that Jesus was the Redeemer of the children of the church. The first tendency pushed the kingdom into the future; the second turned it into an institutional church. The revelators grant that the church as a social outgrowth of the kingdom would have been natural and even desirable. The tragedy is that it almost completely supplanted Jesus' concept of a spiritual brotherhood.

L360.t: Nathaniel's Four Conclusions on the Two Parables
rows: Ability is the practical measure of life's opportunities
Faithfulness is the unerring measure of human trustworthiness
The lesser reward for lesser faithfulness when there is like opportunity
A like reward for like faithfulness when there is lesser opportunity
L360.d: On the last journey up to Jerusalem Jesus told the parable of the pounds, and the apostles asked how it differed from the earlier parable of the talents. Jesus would only say that each should ponder the words and find their true meaning. In later years it was Nathaniel who best taught the meaning of the two parables, summing up his teaching in four conclusions. Ability is the practical measure of life's opportunities, and no one is held responsible for what lies beyond his abilities. Faithfulness is the measure of trustworthiness. With like opportunity, lesser faithfulness earns a lesser reward; with lesser opportunity, like faithfulness earns a like reward. The list comforts: God judges faithfulness within one's opportunity, not the size of the result.

L361.t: Three Reasons the Sadducees Desired to Make Away with Jesus
rows: Popular favor threatened the Jewish nation by possible involvement with the Roman authorities
His zeal for temple reform struck directly at their revenues
They feared the further spread of his new doctrine of the brotherhood of man
L361.d: After Jesus closed his last discourse in the temple with a scathing denunciation of the Jewish rulers, the Sanhedrin formally decreed his death that night. The Sadducees, who then controlled the Sanhedrin, had three reasons for wanting to make away with him. They feared that his popular favor might draw in the Roman authorities and endanger the Jewish nation; his zeal for temple reform and the cleansing of the temple struck directly at their revenues; and, feeling responsible for social order, they feared the spread of his new doctrine of the brotherhood of man. Political fear, economic interest, and social conservatism appear in turn. Unlike the largely religious motives of the Pharisees, the Sadducees' reasons were mostly worldly. A small group of Sadducees even proposed assassination, but the Pharisees refused to countenance it.

L362.t: Four Motives of the Pharisees for Wanting Jesus Put to Death
rows: He was arrayed in telling opposition to their traditional hold upon the people
They held that Jesus was a lawbreaker who disregarded the Sabbath
They charged him with blasphemy because he alluded to God as his Father
His last discourse of bitter denunciation in the temple that day
L362.d: The Pharisees had different motives from the Sadducees for wanting to see Jesus put to death. The revelators give four reasons they feared him. He was arrayed in telling opposition to their traditional hold upon the people; they held him a lawbreaker who disregarded the Sabbath and other ceremonial requirements; they charged him with blasphemy for calling God his Father; and they were thoroughly angry over the bitter denunciation he had delivered in the temple that very day. The list shows how deeply ultraconservative religious teachers can resent attacks upon their vested prestige. The Sanhedrin adjourned near midnight on Tuesday, agreeing to meet the next morning at the home of Caiaphas to formulate the charges.

L363.t: Three Charges Annas Drew from the Temple Saying
rows: A dangerous traducer of the people; he taught impossible things and deceived them
A fanatical revolutionist who advocated laying violent hands on the sacred temple
He taught magic, promising to build a new temple without hands
L363.d: At the Sanhedrist court of inquiry early on Friday morning, shortly after the false witnesses began to testify, Annas arrived and argued that Jesus' threat to destroy the temple warranted three charges: that he was a dangerous traducer who deceived the people, a fanatical revolutionist who advocated violence against the temple, and a teacher of magic who promised to build a new temple without hands. The Sanhedrin had already agreed that Jesus deserved death under Jewish law, but they needed charges that would justify Pilate in pronouncing the death sentence. Yet the decisive moment came when Caiaphas adjured Jesus to say whether he was the Son of God and Jesus answered, "I am." That question of his bestowal mission was the only one he chose to answer.

L364.t: Three Heads of the Indictment of Jesus
rows: A perverter of the Jewish nation; he deceived the people and incited them to rebellion
He taught the people to refuse to pay tribute to Caesar
Claiming to be a king of a new sort of kingdom, he incited treason against the emperor
L364.d: When the Sanhedrist court reassembled at five-thirty on Friday morning, it took only half an hour to draw up the indictment it would bring to Pilate under three heads. Annas had made it clear that the charge of blasphemy would carry no weight with Pilate, so all three were framed as political crimes in Roman eyes: perverting the nation and inciting rebellion, teaching the people to refuse tribute to Caesar, and inciting treason by claiming to be a king. The revelators point out that the entire procedure was irregular and wholly contrary to Jewish law. The charges were formulated without witnesses and in the absence of the accused, and three Pharisees left in protest. The list shows religious hostility putting on the clothing of political accusation.

rows: Perverting our nation and stirring up our people to rebellion
Forbidding the people to pay tribute to Caesar
Calling himself the king of the Jews and teaching the founding of a new kingdom
L365.d: Before Pilate, the high priest and the others signaled the clerk of the court to hand over the written charges. The Sanhedrist tribunal, they said, found Jesus an evildoer and a disturber of the nation, guilty of three things: perverting the nation and stirring up rebellion, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and calling himself king of the Jews while teaching a new kingdom. Yet Jesus had not been regularly tried nor legally convicted on any of these charges, nor had he heard them when first stated. Pilate insisted that they be repeated in Jesus' hearing, but Jesus made no reply to the false charges. Astonished at the unfairness of the proceeding and impressed by Jesus' silent and masterly bearing, Pilate decided to examine him privately. The accusers' fury contrasts with Jesus' sorrowful and compassionate silence.

L366.t: Four Explanations of the Status of Jesus in the Tomb
rows: The Creator consciousness of Michael was at large, wholly free from the mortal mind
The former Thought Adjuster of Jesus was in personal command of the celestial hosts
The acquired spirit identity of the man of Nazareth was consigned to the Paradise Father
The human or mortal consciousness of Jesus slept during these thirty-six hours
L366.d: The physical form of the Master rested in Joseph's tomb until about three o'clock Sunday morning. The revelators confess that they are wholly uncertain about the status of Jesus' personality during those thirty-six hours, and they venture four explanations. The Creator consciousness of Michael was at large and free of the mortal mind; his former Thought Adjuster was on earth in command of the celestial hosts; the spirit identity he acquired during his life in the flesh was consigned to the custody of the Paradise Father; and his human consciousness slept, so that to him the resurrection followed death as of the same instant. The list distinguishes four aspects: Creator, Adjuster, soul, and human consciousness. It is a rare passage in which the revelators openly mark the boundary between knowledge and conjecture.

L367.t: Three Statements Clarifying the Resurrection of Jesus
rows: His material or physical body was not a part of the resurrected personality
He did not emerge from the tomb as a spirit nor as Michael of Nebadon
He came forth in the likeness of the morontia personalities of the first mansion world
L367.d: The revelators propose to "⟦Q 189:1.6⟧forever clarify⟦/Q⟧" the concept of Jesus' resurrection with three statements. First, his physical body was not part of the resurrected personality; he emerged without moving the stones or disturbing Pilate's seals, and his body of flesh remained in the sepulchre. Second, he did not come forth as a spirit nor as Michael of Nebadon, the Creator Sovereign he had been before his incarnation. Third, he came forth in the very likeness of the morontia personalities who emerge from the resurrection halls of the first mansion world. The first two clear away misunderstanding by negation; the third states the positive fact. Unlike the traditional idea of bodily resurrection, Jesus followed the path of his own ascendant creatures, so his resurrection previews the survival of every mortal believer.

L368.t: Seven Factors of Character Weakness in Judas
rows: An isolated type; a confirmed "shut-in" and unsociable sort of person
Life had been made too easy for him; he was a very poor loser
No philosophic technique for meeting disappointment; he blamed others
He was given to holding grudges and entertaining the idea of revenge
He did not like to face facts frankly; dishonest toward life situations
He refused to talk over his difficulties with his real friends or the Master
He never learned that the real rewards for noble living are spiritual prizes
L368.d: The revelators do not treat the betrayal by Judas as a mere event; they trace his defeat in the earth struggle to seven factors of personal tendency and character weakness. He chose isolation, had too easy a childhood and was a poor loser, blamed others for every disappointment, held grudges and nursed revenge, would not face facts honestly, refused to share his problems with his friends or the Master, and never learned that the real rewards of noble living are spiritual. Most of these flow from one root, his persistent isolation of personality. As a result his griefs multiplied and his despair deepened almost beyond endurance. Beyond one man's tragedy, the list is a mirror warning how far common weaknesses can lead when left untended.

L369.t: The Seven Spirits of the Advancing Worlds
rows: The bestowed spirit of the Universal Father
The Thought Adjusters
The spirit presence of the Eternal Son
Spirit gravity of the universe of universes; channel of all spirit communion
The spirit presence of the Infinite Spirit
The universal spirit-mind of all creation
The spirit of the Universal Father and the Creator Son
The Spirit of Truth
The spirit of the Infinite Spirit and the Universe Mother Spirit
The Holy Spirit
The mind-spirit of the Universe Mother Spirit
The seven adjutant mind-spirits of the local universe
The spirit of the Father, Sons, and Spirits
The new-name spirit of ascending mortals after fusion and finality
L369.d: In explaining the outpouring of the Spirit of Truth at Pentecost, the revelators note that mankind is subject to the double influence of the sevenfold appeal of the universe spirit influences. Early evolutionary races are in contact with the seven adjutant mind-spirits of the Universe Mother Spirit, but as man progresses in intelligence and spiritual perception, seven higher spirit influences come to hover over him and dwell within him. They are the Father's Thought Adjusters, the spirit presences of the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit, the Spirit of Truth, the Holy Spirit, the adjutant mind-spirits, and the new-name spirit of ascenders after Adjuster fusion and finality. The list descends from Paradise Deity to the local universe and rises again to the mortal's future. The Spirit of Truth brought the last of these endowments.

L370.t: Five Reasons Christianity Triumphed over the Mystery Cults
rows: Organization; Paul was a great organizer and his successors kept up the pace
Thoroughly Hellenized; the best in Greek philosophy and the cream of Hebrew theology
A new and great ideal, the echo of the life bestowal of Jesus
Compromises with Mithraism won the better half of its adherents
Further compromises with paganism won even the emperor Constantine
L370.d: How did a message of Jewish origin, which had almost failed in the land of its birth, so quickly capture the very best minds of the Roman Empire? The revelators give five reasons for the triumph of Christianity over the philosophic religions and the mystery cults: Paul's organization, a thorough Hellenization embracing Greek philosophy and Hebrew theology, above all the new and great ideal echoing the life bestowal of Jesus, and successive compromises with Mithraism and with paganism. Only the third reason comes from Jesus himself; the rest are strategy and compromise. The revelators judge that early leaders deliberately compromised the ideals of Jesus in order to save many of his ideas, yet they insist that these compromised ideals are still latent in his gospel and will eventually assert their full power upon the world.

L371.t: Four Ways Christianity Gained the Ascendancy
rows: A new and enormously higher note in human morals was struck
A new and greatly enlarged concept of God was given to the world
The hope of immortality became a part of the assurance of a recognized religion
Jesus of Nazareth was given to man's hungry soul
L371.d: In the paganization of Christianity the old order won many minor victories of a ritualistic nature. Yet the revelators say the Christians gained the ascendancy in four greater matters. A new and enormously higher note in human morals was struck, a greatly enlarged concept of God was given to the world, the hope of immortality became part of a recognized religion, and, above all, Jesus of Nazareth was given to man's hungry soul. The outward forms resembled pagan ritual, but the content was incomparably higher. Many truths Jesus taught were almost lost in these compromises, yet they still slumber in Christianity, and the revelators honor Athanasius, who defended the truth of Jesus' nature at Nicaea.

L372.t: Two Things That Caused Christianity to Triumph
rows: The Greek mind was willing to borrow new and good ideas even from the Jews
Paul and his successors were shrewd and sagacious compromisers, keen theologic traders
L372.d: The revelators reduce the rise and triumph of Christianity over all contending religions to two things. One is the openness of the Greek mind, willing to borrow new and good ideas even from the Jews. The other is the skill of Paul and his successors, who were willing but shrewd and sagacious compromisers, keen theologic traders. The first is readiness on the receiving side; the second is adaptation on the giving side. When Paul preached in Athens, the Greeks were spiritually hungry; the Romans at first fought Christianity, but the Greeks embraced it and later forced the Romans to accept it as part of Greek culture. The Greek revered beauty and the Jew holiness, but both loved truth, and under Jesus' message their united thought became the driving power of a new social order.

L373.t: Four High Forms of Thought Distinguished from Religion
rows: Man's logical attitude toward the things of material reality
Man's aesthetic appreciation of beauty contrasted with ugliness
Man's ethical recognition of social obligations and political duty
Even man's sense of human morality is not, in and of itself, religious
L373.d: The revelators define religion as the revelation to man of his divine and eternal destiny, a purely personal and spiritual experience. It must therefore be forever distinguished from man's other high forms of thought: the logical attitude toward material reality, the aesthetic appreciation of beauty contrasted with ugliness, the ethical recognition of social and political duty, and even the sense of human morality, which is not in itself religious. Science, art, ethics, and morals are all valuable, but none can substitute for religion. Religion seeks those values in the universe which call forth faith, trust, and assurance, and it culminates in worship. While the mind discovers relative values, religion discovers supreme values for the soul. The revelators add that no lasting social system can be maintained without a morality predicated on spiritual realities.

L374.t: Seven Events Marking the Master's Progressive Divinization
rows: The arrival of the Thought Adjuster
The messenger of Immanuel who appeared to him at Jerusalem at about twelve
The manifestations attendant upon his baptism
The experiences on the Mount of Transfiguration
The morontia resurrection
The spirit ascension
The final embrace of the Paradise Father, conferring unlimited sovereignty of his universe
L374.d: Just as men must progress from the consciousness of the human to the realization of the divine, so did Jesus ascend from the nature of man to the consciousness of the nature of God. He made this ascent by the conjoint achievement of the faith of his mortal intellect and the acts of his indwelling Adjuster. The revelators say this faith consciousness of progressive divinization passed through seven stages, each marked by an extraordinary event. The arrival of the Adjuster, the messenger of Immanuel at Jerusalem, the baptism, and the Mount of Transfiguration belong to his earth life; the morontia resurrection, the spirit ascension, and the Father's final embrace follow his death. The list presents his life as one ascending process of divine self-realization.

L375.t: Three Evidences of the Spirit Indwelling of the Human Mind
rows: Humanitarian fellowship—love
Only the spirit-indwelt intellect is unselfishly altruistic and unconditionally loving
Interpretation of the universe—wisdom
Only the spirit-indwelt mind comprehends that the universe is friendly to the individual
Spiritual evaluation of life—worship
Only the spirit-indwelt man can realize the divine presence
L375.d: In the final paper of the book the revelators say that the mind of man can attain high levels of spiritual insight because it is not wholly material. There is a spirit nucleus in the mind, the Adjuster of the divine presence, and three separate evidences show this indwelling. An animal mind may be gregarious for self-protection, but only the spirit-indwelt intellect is unselfishly altruistic and unconditionally loving. The same holds for the wisdom that comprehends the universe as friendly to the individual, and for worship that realizes the divine presence and seeks fuller experience of it. The human mind does not create real values; it can only discover, recognize, interpret, and choose. The list offers three experiential signs of God within man.

L376.t: Three Basic Judgments, or Choices, of the Mortal Mind
rows: Self-judgment
Moral choice
Social-judgment
Ethical choice
God-judgment
Religious choice
L376.d: The human mind does not create real values; it discovers, interprets, and chooses them. The revelators teach that the moral values of the universe become intellectual possessions through three basic judgments, or choices, of the mortal mind: self-judgment, which is moral choice; social-judgment, which is ethical choice; and God-judgment, which is religious choice. The object of judgment widens from self to neighbor to God. From this the revelators conclude that all human progress is effected by a technique of conjoint revelational evolution. Unless a divine lover, interpreter, and evaluator lived in man, he could not love spiritually, realize the unity of the universe, or appraise moral values. Human survival depends in great measure on consecrating the will to choosing the values selected by the indwelling spirit.
